Semantic Review in R

Source: vignettes/semantic-review.Rmd
semantic-review.Rmd

create_sdp() produces review-ready metadata. This guide takes you through the 0.5.0 review flow: decide the semantic IRIs, write those decisions, fill the remaining metadata and run strict validation. You can do this from R, keeping your choices in a script. The examples are displayed rather than run when the guide builds; candidate ranks and outstanding fields depend on your package.

Start with a package created by the quickstart:

library(metasalmon)
pkg_path <- "fraser-coho-2023-2024-sdp"

1. Inspect the semantic review queue 

review <- review_semantics(pkg_path)
review

The printed queue groups candidates by the slot they could fill, shows their labels, definitions and ranks, and prints the call that decides each slot. Read the definition against the column’s meaning and methods before accepting. Ranking is a retrieval aid; it does not decide whether a term is appropriate.

review_semantics() reads existing suggestions from the package, a dictionary with a semantic_suggestions attribute, or inferred artifacts. It makes no network or model call. Where those suggestions carry a model’s assessment, ingested from your own harness, it shows it: an accept under the candidate it chose, any other decision once per slot and role. To revisit filled slots, use include_filled = TRUE; use columns = "NATURAL_ADULT_SPAWNERS" to focus on one column. The default shows five candidates for each target, which is one slot or, for a code value, one of its roles; max_candidates = Inf shows all of them.

An empty queue does not establish that the package is finished. A required slot with no retrieved candidates can still appear in review_metadata() below.

2. Accept a candidate or reject the shortlist

Paste the printed call for a candidate you have reviewed. For example, if rank 1 fits the measurement column in your queue:

review <- accept_suggestion(
  review, "NATURAL_ADULT_SPAWNERS", "variable", rank = 1,
  table = "escapement"
)

If no candidate fits, reject that slot and record your actual reason. This example reason is illustrative; replace it with the finding from your review:

review <- reject_suggestion(
  review, "NATURAL_ADULT_SPAWNERS", "unit", table = "escapement",
  reason = "The shortlisted definitions do not match the unit recorded in the source."
)

Each call returns the updated review; neither writes the package yet. A rejection leaves a gap to resolve. It does not approve a different term.

The slot determines the addressing arguments. The printed calls supply them:

Slot Address
A dictionary field column, role; also table when needed
A table-level field role and table, with no column
A code-value field column, role, table and code_value

If a column and its code values share a role, code_value = "" selects the column’s own slot. To accept an independently verified IRI that retrieval did not shortlist, pass it as iri to accept_suggestion(). The setter route in step 4 also handles a field with no candidates.

3. Write and resume your decisions 

apply_sdp_semantics(pkg_path, review)

This writes the decisions into the metadata and keeps datapackage.json in step. Accepted values lose their REVIEW: prefix. Undecided slots remain for review, and data CSV bytes are unchanged. Rejection reasons are persisted in semantic_suggestions.csv and shown with the gap by review_metadata().

Rebuild the queue after writing, or when you return to the package later:

review <- review_semantics(pkg_path)
review

Previously decided slots are omitted by default. Use include_filled = TRUE when you intend to reconsider them.

4. Fill metadata and fields with no candidates 

review_metadata(pkg_path)

This checks the package’s required fields, IRIs and placeholders against the selected schema. It prints setter calls with placeholders for your real values. Replace each placeholder before running a call; an unedited <add ...> value is refused. Review the description and contact details against the source, including permissions and the licence.

The four setters address the four metadata tables. These examples use rows in the bundled quickstart package; adapt the prose to your own source:

set_sdp_dataset(
  pkg_path,
  title = "Fraser coho spawner estimates, 2023-2024",
  description = "Annual spawner estimates by population and survey year."
)

set_sdp_table(
  pkg_path, "escapement",
  table_label = "Spawner estimates",
  description = "Population and year records from the bundled Fraser coho example."
)

set_sdp_column(
  pkg_path, "NATURAL_ADULT_SPAWNERS", table = "escapement",
  column_label = "Natural adult spawners"
)

set_sdp_code(
  pkg_path, "ESTIMATE_STAGE", "FINAL", table = "escapement",
  code_label = "FINAL"
)

These calls illustrate row addressing; they do not fill every outstanding field. set_sdp_column() also accepts term_iri, property_iri, entity_iri and unit_iri; set_sdp_table() accepts observation_unit_iri, and set_sdp_code() accepts term_iri. Supply a term only after checking its meaning and scope. Passing validation does not justify a semantic choice.

The setters write the canonical metadata CSVs and update the descriptor in the same operation. Run review_metadata() again to see what remains.

5. Validate and continue to publication 

review_metadata(pkg_path)
validate_salmon_datapackage(pkg_path, require_iris = TRUE)

Strict validation checks the required metadata and IRIs. Once it passes, you can share the whole SDP folder, keeping its metadata and data files together. EML export and KNB deposit additionally require the reviewed semantic closure and reviewed EML facts. Continue with the post-review publication guide for term gaps, closure evidence and those export and deposit steps. A rejected shortlist or unresolved ontology gap needs a decision before that path can finish.

Have your own harness judge the shortlists

Model judgement runs outside metasalmon. The package writes a review packet, your own harness reads it and writes its answers to a CSV, and the package reads them back. Neither step calls a model; the only network either one reaches is vocabulary search, through search_fn. metasalmonpy writes the same packet, byte for byte apart from its producer member, so one harness serves both packages. The sdp-semantic-review skill of the smn-sci-plgn plugin is a ready-made harness for Claude Code and Codex; Semantic Review in Your Harness shows that route. This section shows what any harness does, so you can write your own.

packet <- write_semantic_review_packet(pkg_path, context_files = "methods-note.md")
packet$path      # <package>/review/semantic-review-packet.json
packet$packet_id # the SHA-256 the ingester checks

The packet holds exactly the slots review_semantics() would queue, each with its shortlist retrieved again (top_n = 5 by default) and the evidence the package’s own validators read: label, IRI, source, native type, role hints, definition and scores. It also holds the measurement bundles with their current slots, scored excerpts from your context files, the review instructions, and the 30-column answer schema, which names an owner for every column. It is written under review/, which no publication path reads.

The harness answers every slot with one of five decisions: accept (giving the candidate’s index and echoing its IRI), review, retry_search (with a short query), reject_shortlist or request_new_term. It writes them, with a CSV library, to review/semantic-assessments-pass-1.csv, and writes the packet’s packet_id to the one-line sidecar semantic-assessments-pass-1.csv.packet-id beside it. The packet’s instructions member is the full brief. The shape of a harness, written here in R with the judgement left to yours:

review_packet <- jsonlite::read_json(packet$path)
columns <- vapply(review_packet$output$columns, `[[`, character(1), "name")
answer <- file.path(pkg_path, review_packet$output$file)

rows <- list()
for (unit in review_packet$units) {
  for (slot in unit$slots) {
    row <- stats::setNames(as.list(rep("", length(columns))), columns)
    identity <- lapply(slot$identity, function(value) if (is.null(value)) "" else value)
    row[names(identity)] <- identity
    row$llm_provider <- "my-harness"
    row$llm_model <- "my-model"
    # judge() is yours. It returns a named list with llm_decision and
    # llm_confidence, and for an accept llm_selected_candidate_index and
    # llm_selected_iri.
    verdict <- judge(unit, slot)
    row[names(verdict)] <- verdict
    rows[[length(rows) + 1L]] <- tibble::as_tibble(row)
  }
}
readr::write_csv(dplyr::bind_rows(rows), answer, na = "")
writeLines(review_packet$packet_id, paste0(answer, ".packet-id"))

Then read the answers back:

result <- ingest_semantic_assessments(pkg_path)
result$status # "complete", or "awaiting_pass_2"
assessments <- semantic_llm_assessments(pkg_path)

The ingester checks the file against the packet it names, then each row. An IRI the packet did not offer is recorded as an error and never applied, a candidate index that is not a whole number is refused, and a final reject_shortlist is escalated to request_new_term, so the ontology gap is filed rather than lost. The record is kept in review/semantic-llm-assessments.csv. A retry_search whose search finds new candidates writes a second packet, review/semantic-review-packet-pass-2.json: answer it in semantic-assessments-pass-2.csv the same way and call ingest_semantic_assessments() again. Nothing from that slot is merged until then, and there is no third pass.

Nothing the harness writes reaches the metadata. The ingester never touches the metadata CSVs; you confirm each answer in the review queue, where the harness’s verdict now sits under the candidate it chose:

── spawners · spawner_count · variable ───────────────────────────────────────
   field:   column_dictionary.csv · term_iri
   current: REVIEW: https://w3id.org/smn/SpawnerAbundance

   [1] Spawner Abundance   smn   score 4.9
       Mature salmon returning to spawn.
       https://w3id.org/smn/SpawnerAbundance
       llm: accept (confidence 0.9)
            Matches the column's definition.
       review <- accept_suggestion(review, "spawner_count", "variable", rank = 1)

A decision other than accept is printed once, under current:, because it judges the whole shortlist. Accept or reject as in section 2, then write your decisions as in section 3.

For a dictionary you have not written yet, pass it in place of the path, with a review_dir for the session’s files: write_semantic_review_packet(dict, review_dir = "review"), then ingest_semantic_assessments(dict, review_dir = "review"). Its result$dictionary carries the assessments, so review_semantics() and apply_semantic_suggestions(..., strategy = "llm") read them from there.

Spreadsheet fallback

You can still edit metadata/*.csv in a spreadsheet, save them as CSV and run validation again. Preserve row keys and column names. This route requires you to keep the reasoning for your choices alongside the package; the R decision calls record shortlist rejections directly. Neither route makes a retrieved term or a passing validator a substitute for checking the source meaning.
